newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia stops Sarajevo-Belgrade bus service.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia stops Sarajevo-Belgrade bus service.

text.p: The Bosnian government plans to halt a newly reopened Sarajevo-Belgrade bus service, accusing Yugoslav authorities of violating an agreement establishing the route, the Sarajevo bus company Centrotrans said on Tuesday.
Centrotrans said it had been told of the decision, effective from Wednesday, by Bosnia's foreign trade and communications ministry, which objected to several Yugoslav measures.

The bus service, which reopened two weeks ago for the first time since war broke out in Bosnia in 1992, was agreed as part of negotiations establishing diplomatic relations between Bosnia and rump Yugoslavia, which is made up of Serbia and Montenegro.

Since its inaugural run to Belgrade on October 15, the bus line has encountered problems on Serb-controlled territory and at the Bosnia-Yugoslav border. On the first day, buses were held up for several hours at the frontier while Yugoslav police demanded payment for tourist visas and refused to allow men of military age to enter Yugoslavia.
The bilateral agreement between the two countries had envisaged visaless travel.
After October 19, passengers were forced to leave the Sarajevo bus and move to a Belgrade bus once they reached Bosnian Serb controlled-territory near former front lines, a Centrotrans official said.

"It was no longer an international bus line as agreed, but a local line reaching the front line between Tuzla and Bijeljina, where passengers would go into (Belgrade bus company) Lasta's bus," Amir Poturovic told Reuters.
"Each passenger was also being charged 53 German marks ($35) for some tourist visa to enter Yugoslavia and we could not take any men of military age on the bus," he said.

He also said that Centrotrans buses had been charged 450 marks for each entry into Yugoslavia and were given provisional registration plates, because the police said Sarajevo plates were not permitted inside the country.

To avoid paying border fees, the two transport companies agreed to exchange passengers at Ban Brdo, which lies on a former front line between government-held Tuzla and Serb-held Bijeljina in northeastern Bosnia, Poturovic said.
The Moslem president of Bosnia's collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic agreed to establish full diplomatic relations in talks last month in Paris.

During 43 months of war in Bosnia, Serbia armed Bosnian Serb forces opposed to the Bosnian government's bid for independence from old Yugoslavia. A peace agreement divides Bosnia into Serb and Moslem-Croat territories governed by a inter-ethnic presidency and parliament.
